Subject: Performance SLOs & autoscaling — quick recap + next steps

Alex — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap from my side and the next steps we discussed so we have everything in one place.

Key SLOs you called out:
- P95 latency target: <= 200ms for streaming responses (end-to-end, client-visible).
- Throughput: baseline ~50 req/s, sustained peaks ~120 req/s, burst to ~1,000 req/s for short windows (3-5 min).
- Concurrency: want support for ~200 concurrent live sessions per region.
- Streaming requirements: token-by-token streaming to clients (low tail latencies).

Autoscaling / burst requirements we noted:
- Scale-up time target: ideally <60s to avoid impacting SLOs for common bursts.
- Warm pool: prefer warm capacity to handle frequent small bursts (you mentioned wanting 8-12 warm workers).
- Queueing: acceptable short queueing (<30s) for very large bursts, but minimal tail latency for streaming.

Action items / next steps:
1) We'll provide a short SLO guidance doc and a recommended autoscale configuration based on the patterns you shared.
2) Dev (cc'd) to run through warm-pool + scale-up times for the model class you mentioned and propose a design.
3) You to share historical load traces / the CSV you mentioned so we can validate sizing.

If that all looks right, I'd like to schedule a technical deep-dive with Dev and your infra folks this week — suggest Wed 21 Jul 10:00am PT or Thu 22 Jul 11:00am PT. What works best?

Thanks,

- The sustained 120 req/s number is what we see during business hours for our primary use case. Bursts to ~1,000 req/s happen about 2-3x per week for 3-5 minutes (ad campaigns, product launches).
- Typical average sequence length is ~120 tokens; worst-case 512 tokens for a handful of queries.
- We need token-by-token streaming to client web sockets; any buffering at the platform level is OK as long as client-visible stall is <200ms p95.

Subject: Re: Performance SLOs & autoscaling — quick recap + next steps

Alex / Marissa — quick technical summary ahead of the deep-dive (attached: redwood-autoscale-design.pdf). High-level answers to the items you flagged:

1) Scale-up times:
- Provisioning new GPU-backed workers (cold): ~60-90s depending on instance type and region.
- Warm-pool activation (pre-warmed model in memory): ~4-8s to accept traffic on an existing warm worker.
- KV cache population for large sequence lengths can add ~1-3s for first token-heavy sessions; subsequent requests benefit from cache.

2) Warm pool recommendations:
- For their burst profile (short 3-5min spikes to 1k req/s) we recommend a hybrid approach: keep a small warm pool per-region (8 warm workers) sized for common bursts and rely on ephemeral workers to scale the remainder.
- Warm pool sizing tradeoff: 8 warm workers covers ~200-300 req/s depending on model variant/seq length; increasing to 12 reduces tail risk but raises committed cost.

3) Queueing & tail-latency controls:
- We use a multi-priority queue: interactive streaming traffic gets highest priority; background/batch calls can be deprioritized.
- Token-level backpressure and early throttling reduce resource contention when a large backlog forms.
- For very large bursts we can allow short queues (up to 30s) with graceful degradation (drop to lower-fidelity model variant or apply rate limits with clear 429 responses).

4) Can we meet the SLO?
- For streaming p95 <= 200ms we need to validate the model variant (quantized vs full FP16) and confirm average sequence length. With a warm-pool + prioritized queues, we believe this is achievable for the majority of traffic; long-tail worst-case requests (512 tokens, heavy context) will need mitigation (model variant fallback or pre-warm).

Next steps before the call:
- Alex: anything else you can attach about model variant and typical seq lengths will help.
- Marissa: I'll bring a short perf-run checklist and a sketch of the autoscale config to validate on the call.

Attached: redwood-autoscale-design.pdf (design + estimated scale-up curves).

Thanks,
